passages.text:
Parliament has cleared the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026, which changes a law on the rights of transgender persons enacted in 2019. The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in mid-March 2026 by Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar, whose ministry administers the 2019 law. Its central change is to omit the provision that gives transgender persons the right to self-perceived gender identity. That right rests on a landmark Supreme Court judgment, which held that gender identity could be recognised without sex reassignment surgery and also recognised a third gender category.

The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on 24 March 2026 by voice vote, amid a walkout by the Opposition. Replying to the debate, Virendra Kumar said the legislation was meant to protect people facing discrimination on the basis of biological factors. He told the House that district magistrates would issue identity certificates to transgender persons, and that a medical board would assist in the identification process.

The Bill also introduces graded punishments for offences against transgender persons. Forcing a person into a transgender identity, or compelling a person to beg or work in servitude, attracts heavier penalties under the amended text, with higher penalties where the victim is a child. Critics said the medical boards and magistrate-issued certificates would add bureaucratic hurdles for people seeking recognition.

The Rajya Sabha took up the Bill the next day. On 25 March 2026, the Upper House passed it by voice vote after rejecting a motion to refer the Bill to a select parliamentary committee. Opposition members alleged that the Bill excluded gay and lesbian persons, and argued that it went against the Supreme Court's earlier ruling on self-identification. The government maintained that the changes were needed to protect people on the basis of biological and physiological characteristics.

President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent to the Bill on 30 March 2026, and it became the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026. The 2019 Act had been passed by Parliament to give statutory form to the rights recognised by the Supreme Court. Reports on the amended law say it narrows the definition of transgender persons to those with certain biological or physiological characteristics, intersex variations, or socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, and makes medical certification a requirement for recognition. Opponents said the changes reduce the protection that transgender persons had enjoyed under the 2019 law.

Under the 2019 Act, a person applied to the District Magistrate for a certificate, and that certificate conferred the right to self-perceived gender identity. The 2026 amendment changes that route. The Opposition, including the Congress, described the Bill as an unconstitutional regression, and some members argued that the Bill left sexual orientation out of its scope.

questions.q: The landmark Supreme Court judgment that recognised the right to self-perceived gender identity was delivered in which year?
questions.explanation: The NALSA judgment, which upheld self-perceived gender identity and recognised a third gender, was delivered in 2014. The 2019 Act was enacted to build on it. The passage does not give the year.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution of India does the President give or withhold assent to a Bill passed by Parliament?
questions.explanation: Article 111 deals with assent to Bills: the President must either give assent or withhold it, and a non-Money Bill may be returned once for reconsideration. Article 110 defines Money Bills.

questions.assertion: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 became law after the President gave assent on 30 March 2026.
questions.reason: Under Article 111, the President must either give assent to a Bill passed by Parliament or withhold assent, and may return a non-Money Bill once for reconsideration.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but R states the general procedure under Article 111 and does not explain why assent was given on 30 March 2026. So R is not the reason for A.

list2: A. Procedure for amending the Constitution
B. Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights
D. Protection of life and personal liberty
questions.explanation: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; Article 32 lets a person move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Part III rights; Article 111 covers assent to Bills; Article 368 sets the amendment procedure.

statements: I. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 came into force on 10 January 2020.
II. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 was passed by Parliament in 2020.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true: the Act came into force on 10 January 2020 by notification S.O. 135(E). Statement II is false: Parliament passed the Act in 2019, and it received presidential assent on 5 December 2019.

statements: 1. A Bill to amend the Constitution must be passed in each House by a majority of its total membership and by a majority of at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
2. Under Article 111, the President may return a Bill other than a Money Bill to the Houses for reconsideration.
3. Under Article 32, only the High Courts can issue writs to enforce fundamental rights.
4. The President may withhold assent to a constitutional amendment Bill that has been passed by both Houses with the required majority.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct (Article 368(2) and the Article 111 proviso). Statement 3 is wrong because Article 32 is a Supreme Court power, while High Courts have writ power under Article 226. Statement 4 is wrong because Article 368(2) says the President shall give assent. Two statements are incorrect.

Supreme Court warns against AI-generated fake judgments
passages.text:
The Supreme Court of India has treated reliance on non-existent, artificial intelligence-generated judgments as a serious judicial lapse. On 27 February 2026, the Court said that a decision resting on such fake case law is not merely an error in decision-making but amounts to misconduct, and that legal consequences would follow.

The case began as an ordinary civil dispute. It arose from an injunction suit over a property, in which a trial court passed an order in August 2025 dismissing the defendants' challenge to a report filed by an Advocate Commissioner. That order relied on four decisions which the petitioners said did not exist and had been generated using artificial intelligence. The High Court, after noting that the judgments were AI-generated, went on to decide the matter on its merits, dismissed the civil revision petition, and issued a word of caution.

The Supreme Court's order went further. Pending disposal of the petition before it, the Court stayed any reliance on the Advocate Commissioner's report and directed that the trial court shall not proceed on the basis of that report. The Court issued notice to the Attorney General for India, the Solicitor General of India and the Bar Council of India, asking for their responses on the issue.

To assist it in examining the question in detail, the Court appointed senior advocate Shyam Divan as amicus curiae. The notice was made returnable on 10 March 2026, when the matter was listed for further hearing.

The case puts a basic question before the highest court in the country: how a citation is verified before it is relied upon in a judicial decision, and who bears responsibility when a citation turns out to be fictitious. Judges depend on counsel and on the record placed before them, and the Court's order makes clear that the source of an authority matters as much as the reasoning built upon it. The notices to the Attorney General, the Solicitor General and the Bar Council of India mean that each will be heard on the issue, and the amicus's assistance is expected to shape any guidance the Court may later consider for advocates and courts.

For practising lawyers, the episode is a reminder that every authority cited in a petition, a written submission or an order must be checked against the official report before it is placed on the record. For litigants, the stay on the Advocate Commissioner's report shows that a decision built on unreliable material can be halted before it takes effect. The order does not yet settle the consequences for the trial court or the High Court. Those questions will depend on the responses the Court receives and on the findings it makes once the petition is decided, and until then the stay on the Advocate Commissioner's report remains in force.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution of India is the Supreme Court declared a court of record, with power to punish for contempt of itself?
questions.explanation: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a Court of Record with power to punish for contempt of itself. The passage does not mention the Article. Article 124 sets the qualifications for Supreme Court judges, as the Article 76 commentary notes, and is not the court-of-record provision.

questions.q: The Attorney General for India is provided for under Article 76. For appointment as Attorney General, the Constitution requires the same qualifications as for a judge of which court?
questions.explanation: Article 76 ties eligibility for the office of Attorney General to the qualifications for appointment as a Supreme Court judge, which are set out in Article 124. The passage names the Attorney General but does not state the eligibility rule.

questions.assertion: A High Court can issue writs for purposes that go beyond the enforcement of fundamental rights.
questions.reason: Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Part III rights and for any other purpose.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. Article 226 allows writs for 'any other purpose', which is the textual basis for the High Court's wider writ jurisdiction compared with Article 32, so the reason explains the assertion.

list2: B. Supreme Court as a court of record
C. High Court as a court of record
D. Writs for enforcement of fundamental rights by the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court power to issue writs for enforcement of Part III rights (I-D). Article 76 provides for the Attorney General (II-A). Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a court of record (III-B). Article 215 makes each High Court a court of record (IV-C). Sources: Article 32 bare act, Article 76, Article 129 and Article 215 pages.

statements: I. The Bar Council of India is constituted under section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961.
II. Article 215 declares the Supreme Court a court of record and empowers it to punish for contempt of itself.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true: section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961 provides for the Bar Council of India, as the Act's table of contents shows. Statement II is false: the Supreme Court's court-of-record status is in Article 129, while Article 215 concerns the High Courts.

statements: 1. Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a court of record.
2. Article 215 declares each High Court a court of record.
3. The Attorney General for India is provided for under Article 124.
4. Article 226 empowers a High Court to issue writs only for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is incorrect because the Attorney General is provided for under Article 76; Article 124 sets qualifications for Supreme Court judges. Statement 4 is incorrect because Article 226 also covers 'any other purpose'. Two statements are incorrect, so the answer is 'Only two'.

passages.title: Botswana cheetahs reach Kuno
passages.text:
Nine cheetahs from Botswana arrived at Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh on February 28, 2026, adding a new international batch to Project Cheetah, the programme that is bringing the big cat back to Indian forests. Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav welcomed the animals at the park, and All India Radio carried the report the same evening. Reports at the time put India's cheetah population at 48 after the arrival, a figure that has since risen.

The move came about three months after the handover. On November 13, 2025, Botswana formally handed over eight cheetahs to India at Mokolodi Nature Reserve, near Gaborone, during the state visit of President Droupadi Murmu. The cheetahs had been brought from the Ghanzi region in the Kalahari desert and included adults and sub-adults. Officials from both countries briefed the two presidents at the ceremony, and the Ministry of External Affairs said the transfer was made under the next phase of Project Cheetah. President Murmu said the animals would join their relatives at Kuno National Park. Officials described the handover as a boost to wildlife cooperation between the two countries.

The nine animals were welcomed at Kuno on February 28, and Yadav released them into quarantine enclosures there. Officials said they would undergo health monitoring and acclimatisation before being moved to larger soft-release areas, and that they would not be moved into the open until that period ended. Acclimatisation gives reintroduced animals time to adjust to a new habitat and food supply before they roam freely, which is why the step is standard in translocation work. Yadav described the arrival in a social media post.

The Botswana group follows earlier batches, and the programme has relied on African partners for its animals. The cheetah had been absent from India for decades before the reintroduction began. In September 2022, eight cheetahs from an African country were released at Kuno, the first batch under the programme. A flight carrying a second batch of 12 cheetahs from South Africa took off in February 2023, and those animals were also taken to Kuno.

Kuno National Park spreads across Sheopur district in Madhya Pradesh and lies in the Gwalior Chambal region. Its core area covers about 748.76 square kilometres, and the park takes its name from the Kuno River that flows through it.

Further transfers are under discussion. Business Standard reported in September 2025 that talks were under way with Botswana, Namibia and Kenya to translocate 8 to 10 cheetahs from each country. India and Botswana had also announced a cheetah translocation pact before the November handover.

The national count has changed since February. On October 5, 2026, five cubs were born at Kuno, taking the national total to 60.

questions.q: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, which governs the protection of wild animals in India, was enacted in which year?
questions.explanation: The Wild Life (Protection) Act was enacted in 1972 (Act No. 53 of 1972). The passage does not mention the Act; the answer is static GK on the statute protecting the animals in the passage.

questions.q: In which year did the Government of India officially declare the cheetah extinct in the country?
questions.explanation: The cheetah was officially declared extinct in India in 1952. The passage refers to the species only as having been absent for decades, so the year must come from outside the passage.

list1: I. Range of the Asiatic cheetah subspecies
II. IUCN Red List status of the cheetah species
III. IUCN Red List status of the Asiatic cheetah subspecies
IV. Mature cheetah individuals estimated by the IUCN (2021 assessment)
questions.explanation: The Asiatic cheetah (A. j. venaticus) is found in Iran and is rated Critically Endangered by the IUCN. The cheetah species as a whole is rated Vulnerable, with an estimated 6,517 mature individuals in the 2021 assessment.

questions.assertion: India's cheetah reintroduction has relied on batches brought from more than one African country.
questions.reason: The first batch of cheetahs brought to India for Project Cheetah came from Namibia in 2022.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true: batches came from Namibia, South Africa and Botswana. The Namibian origin of the first batch is not a reason for the reliance on several countries, so R is true but does not explain A.

statements: I. The Asiatic cheetah subspecies is rated Critically Endangered by the IUCN.
II. The cheetah species as a whole is rated Least Concern by the IUCN.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true (Asiatic cheetah, Iran, Critically Endangered). Statement II is false: the cheetah species is rated Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.

statements: 1. The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1947.
2. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted in 1972.
3. The cheetah species as a whole is rated Critically Endangered by the IUCN.
4. The cheetah species as a whole is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect: the extinction was declared in 1952, and the species is rated Vulnerable, not Critically Endangered. Statements 2 and 4 are correct, so the answer is Only two.

passages.title: Women AutHer Awards 2026 and Urmila Pawar
passages.text:
The seventh edition of the Women AutHer Awards, a literary prize for women authors, announced its winners in April 2026, with veteran actor and author Kabir Bedi as chief guest. The awards are a joint venture between JK Paper and The Times of India, according to a PrintWeek report dated 8 April 2026. Juries chose most of the winners, while the popular choice award was decided through online voting. Each winning author received Rs 1 lakh, and prize money was shared equally where there were joint winners.

Kavery Nambisan won the fiction award for Rising Sons. Likla Lall took the children's books award for Ganesh Haloi: Colours of Home. In nonfiction, Vidya Rajan was honoured for Rubber: The Social and Natural History of an Indispensable Substance, and Narayani Basu for A Man For All Seasons, a biography of KM Panikkar. The debut awards went to Swati Pandey for Invisible in Plain Sight: Voices From the By-Lanes of Kamathipura and to Subi Taba for Tales from the Dawn-Lit Mountains. Astha Gill's Blame it on the Hormones won the popular choice award, and Saanvi Shabeesh's City of Doom won for best manuscript.

The lifetime achievement award went to Urmila Pawar, a Marathi writer best known for her autobiography, The Weave of My Life: A Dalit Woman's Memoirs. Her Marathi original, Aaydan, which means bamboo basketry, first appeared in 2003. The English edition is a translation by Maya Pandit, an experienced translator of women's writing from Marathi who is pro-vice chancellor of the English and Foreign Language University in Hyderabad. The title uses weaving as a metaphor for writing an autobiography.

The memoir follows three generations of Mahar Dalit women, beginning with Pawar's childhood in a small village on the Konkan coast. It describes caste discrimination, poverty and gender-based oppression, both in mainstream society and within the Dalit community itself. It covers how her community encountered Ambedkarite ideas and converted to Buddhism, and it recounts her marriage to Harishchandra and the family's move to the city. Pawar holds an MA from the University of Bombay and spent many years in the labour welfare department of the Government of Maharashtra before turning to writing.

Reviewers have noted the candour of the book, particularly its frank account of familial and marital conflict, which upset some of her admirers. The jury praised her honest and deep writing on identity, equality and justice, and said her work gives voice to stories that often go unheard. Scroll.in reported the results, and the seventh edition drew some of the biggest names in the literary world to the ceremony. Pawar's honour came alongside prizes for debut fiction, popular choice and best manuscript, and her Marathi memoir, first published in 2003, was honoured in the same ceremony as the new English-language titles.

questions.q: On what date did B. R. Ambedkar convert to Buddhism in a mass ceremony at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur?
questions.explanation: Ambedkar converted to Buddhism at Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur on 14 October 1956; the annual observance is Dhammachakra Pravartan Din. The other options are distractors and are not supported by the source.

questions.q: In which year was the Sahitya Akademi, India's National Academy of Letters, formally inaugurated by the Government of India?
questions.explanation: The Akademi's official website states it was formally inaugurated on 12 March 1954. It was registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 7 January 1956, which is why 1956 is a distractor.

questions.assertion: Urmila Pawar's The Weave of My Life is an English translation of a work originally written in Marathi.
questions.reason: Marathi is written in the Devanagari script.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, but the Devanagari script does not explain why the book is a translation; the translation relationship rests on Marathi being the original language, not its script. Hence R is true but not the explanation of A.

list1: II. The God of Small Things
questions.explanation: Rushdie won the Booker Prize in 1981 for Midnight's Children; Arundhati Roy won in 1997 for The God of Small Things; Jhabvala won in 1975 for Heat and Dust; William Golding won in 1980 for Rites of Passage.

statements: I. Marathi is the official language of Maharashtra.
II. Marathi is written in the Modi script.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true. Statement II is false: Marathi is written in Devanagari, the official writing system; Modi was a historical script used for administration and business records.

statements: 1. Arundhati Roy won the 1997 Booker Prize for her debut novel, The God of Small Things.
2. Salman Rushdie won the Booker Prize for Midnight's Children in 1980.
3. Ambedkar's mass conversion to Buddhism took place on 14 October 1956.
4. The Sahitya Akademi was registered as a society on 12 March 1956.
questions.explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong because the Booker Prize for Midnight's Children is recorded under 1981 (Booker prize-year page). Statement 4 is wrong because the Akademi was formally inaugurated on 12 March 1954 and registered as a society on 7 January 1956. Two statements are incorrect: Only two.

passages.title: India tests Agni missiles in May 2026
passages.text:
India carried out a flight test of an advanced Agni missile fitted with MIRV technology on 8 May 2026, the Ministry of Defence said in a statement. The launch took place from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island, off the coast of Odisha, which hosts the Integrated Test Range, the country's main missile testing complex. The missile carried multiple payloads, each aimed at a different target spread over a large geographical area in the Indian Ocean Region. Telemetry from several ground-based and ship-based stations tracked the entire trajectory, from lift-off until the impact of all payloads. The ministry said all mission objectives were met.

The missile was developed by DRDO laboratories with the support of industries across the country. Senior DRDO scientists and Indian Army personnel witnessed the trial. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh congratulated DRDO, the Army and the participating industries. He said the test would add a significant capability to the country's defence preparedness in the face of growing threat perceptions. The official statements did not give the missile's range, the number of payloads or the exact target locations.

Two weeks later, on 22 May 2026, the Ministry announced a second launch. An Agni-1 short-range ballistic missile was test-launched from the Integrated Test Range at Chandipur, Odisha. The trial was carried out under the aegis of the Strategic Forces Command, and the ministry said the launch validated all operational and technical parameters of the missile.

Reports on the Agni-1 launch placed the Strategic Forces Command at the centre of India's nuclear command arrangements. Swarajya described it as a critical component of the Nuclear Command Authority. The same report said the May launch followed a similar trial in July 2025, and that the advanced Agni missile with MIRV technology had been tested on 8 May.

The island that hosted the 8 May trial was named after former President APJ Abdul Kalam, who had served as the first director of the test range. Before the renaming, it was known by a British colonial name. The land was handed to the Defence Research and Development Organisation for missile testing, and a Prithvi missile test landed on the island in 1993. Test ranges on the Odisha coast have since hosted launches of several systems, including the Akash, Prithvi and Agni missiles.

Some details remain unclear. One report dated the Agni-1 launch to 21 May, while most sources give 22 May. Some reports also describe the Chandipur site differently, placing it in Balasore district. The 8 May date appears in both the ministry statement and DRDO's own post, and the 22 May date is confirmed by the ministry. The official statements focused on mission outcomes rather than technical specifications, so performance data for both missiles remain limited to what the ministry released in its announcements.

questions.q: In which year was the island that hosted the 8 May 2026 Agni trial renamed Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island?
questions.explanation: The island, formerly Wheeler Island, was renamed on 4 September 2015 to honour former President APJ Abdul Kalam.

questions.q: On which date was the Strategic Forces Command, which conducted the 22 May 2026 Agni-1 test, created?
questions.explanation: The Cabinet Committee on Security approved the creation of the Strategic Forces Command, with a Commander-in-Chief, on 4 January 2003.

questions.assertion: The Agni-1 test of 22 May 2026 was carried out under the Strategic Forces Command.
questions.reason: The Strategic Forces Command is an integrated tri-service command responsible for managing and administering India's strategic forces.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true. The reason explains the assertion: the command that manages the strategic forces is the one that conducted the launch.

list1: I. Executive Council of the Nuclear Command Authority
II. Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority
III. Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island
list2: A. Chaired by the National Security Adviser
B. Located in Bhadrak district, Odisha
D. Chaired by the Prime Minister
questions.explanation: The Executive Council is chaired by the National Security Adviser and the Political Council by the Prime Minister. The island lies in Bhadrak district, and Agni-I is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile.

statements: I. The Agni-I missile was first launched from a road mobile launcher at the Integrated Test Range on Wheeler Island on 25 January 2002.
II. The Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority is chaired by the Defence Minister.
questions.explanation: Statement I is true. Statement II is false: the Political Council is chaired by the Prime Minister, so only I is correct.

statements: 1. Only the Political Council of the Nuclear Command Authority can authorise the use of nuclear weapons.
2. The Executive Council of the Nuclear Command Authority is chaired by the Chief of Defence Staff.
3. The Strategic Forces Command is headed by a Commander-in-Chief.
4. The Nuclear Command Authority's 2003 framework was approved by the Cabinet Committee on Security on 4 January 2003.
questions.explanation: Only statement 2 is incorrect: the Executive Council is chaired by the National Security Adviser. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, so exactly one statement is incorrect.
